lessons.title: What Jurisprudence Asks
body: Jurisprudence is the philosophical study of law. Lawyers usually ask what the law is on a particular point: does this contract bind, is this search lawful. Philosophers ask what makes anything law at all, what law is for, and when it deserves obedience. The subject divides into three broad kinds of question.

The first is analytical, or conceptual: what is the nature of law, and how does it differ from commands of a gunman, rules of etiquette, or the rules of a club? A related question is validity, meaning what makes a particular rule part of the legal system. Different theories answer by pointing to different things: the will of a sovereign, a basic norm, social practice among officials, moral truth, or the predictions of how courts will actually decide.

The second is normative: what ought the law to be, what should it permit or forbid, and what justifies punishment, taxation or property? Here jurisprudence meets political philosophy and ethics. Theories of justice, rights and punishment belong in this part of the subject.

The third concerns adjudication and interpretation: how do judges decide hard cases, how much room do they have, and how should they read texts and precedents? Theories of formalism, realism, originalism and Dworkin's interpretivism all give answers.

A useful way to hold the map in mind is the contest over the connection between law and morality. Natural law theorists claim there is some necessary connection: an extremely unjust enactment fails in some way to be law, or at least to be law in the fullest sense. Legal positivists claim that whether something is law depends on social facts, such as who made it and how, and not on whether it is good. The positivist can still say that bad laws should be disobeyed. The claim is about the identification of law, not about its worth. Realists and critical schools raise a different challenge: the official story about neutral rules hides the way power, politics and interests shape legal outcomes.

Two warnings help from the start. Labels cover families of views, and individual authors often reject part of the family portrait. And these debates are not only abstract. When a judge says that the plain text controls, that a statute cannot mean something absurd, that a principle of fairness limits a rule, or that a punishment is excessive, she is taking a position that jurisprudence has named and studied.

This course takes each school on its own terms before examining the criticisms, because a theory is easiest to judge once its strongest version is on the table. It also keeps law's contested political questions separate from the question of what the law currently is, since the philosophy asks how to reason about such questions, not what to conclude.

Worked example: a statute bans vehicles in a park. A police officer stops a child on a tricycle. A positivist asks whether the statute was validly enacted and what its words and practice settle. A natural lawyer may ask about the law's purpose. A realist asks how the local judges will actually rule. A critical scholar asks whose interests the rule serves. Each question is legitimate, and each school is best at one of them.

lessons.title: The Natural Law Tradition
body: Natural law theory holds that law has a necessary connection to morality, and that there are standards of right that do not depend on what any human legislature says. The idea is old and takes several forms. Aristotle, in the Nicomachean Ethics, distinguished what is just by nature from what is just by convention, although he treated the natural as changeable in human affairs. The Stoics and Cicero in the Roman world described a law of reason, the same everywhere, binding all rational beings, which no state can repeal. Cicero's account in On the Republic and On the Laws is the classic source for the claim that a state without justice is not a true commonwealth.

Thomas Aquinas, in the thirteenth century, gave the tradition its most influential structure in the Summa Theologiae. He distinguished four kinds of law: eternal law, the divine reason governing the whole creation; natural law, the participation of rational creatures in eternal law, accessible by reason; divine law, given by revelation; and human law, the particular rules made by communities. Human law derives its force from natural law in two ways. Some of its rules are conclusions drawn from natural precepts, as the ban on murder follows from the precept to do no harm. Others are determinations, specifications of what nature leaves open, as the rule to drive on one side of the road settles a coordination problem.

For Aquinas a human law that conflicts with natural law is not a law in the full sense but a corruption or perversion of law. A famous slogan, often traced to Augustine, says that an unjust law is no law at all. Scholars debate how strong a claim this is. A moderate reading says unjust enactments lack the moral binding force of law and do not generate a duty of obedience, though people may still obey them to avoid scandal or disorder. The strong reading says such enactments are not legally valid. Many natural lawyers adopt the moderate reading.

Natural law arguments have played a prominent role in public life. Early modern thinkers such as Grotius and Locke developed natural rights from the tradition, which later shaped declarations of rights. Opponents of slavery and later of racial segregation invoked a higher law, and the Nuremberg trials after the Second World War relied on the idea that some acts are criminal even when ordered or legalized by a regime.

Objections come from several directions. Positivists object that the thesis confuses what the law is with what it ought to be, which makes it harder to see and say clearly that an evil regime had laws. Skeptics argue that people disagree about the content of natural law, so it cannot provide the common standard it promises. Defenders reply that disagreement does not show there is no truth, and that the theory's claim is about the structure of practical reasoning: law is a rational enterprise aimed at the common good, so a rule that serves nothing of the sort is defective as law.

Worked example: a regime enacts a statute requiring citizens to report neighbors for harboring refugees, with severe penalties for failing to report. A strong natural lawyer says it lacks legal validity. A moderate one says it is law in a thin sense but not binding in conscience. A positivist says it is law but morally monstrous and ought to be disobeyed.

lessons.title: Modern Natural Law: Fuller, Finnis and Radbruch
body: Twentieth-century natural law theory shifted from theology to the structure of law itself. Lon Fuller, in The Morality of Law (1964), argued that law is a purposive activity, the enterprise of subjecting human conduct to the governance of rules, and that this purpose generates an internal morality. He identified eight ways in which a legal system can fail: failing to make rules at all and deciding ad hoc; failing to publicize the rules; abusing retroactive legislation; failing to make rules understandable; enacting contradictory rules; requiring conduct beyond the powers of the affected party; changing the rules so often that people cannot orient themselves; and a failure of congruence between the rules as announced and their actual administration. He called these principles of legality. Fuller thought that a system that failed totally would not be law, and that a regime committed to such principles would be pressed, at the margin, toward fairness. He called this an internal, procedural natural law.

Fuller's fable of the Speluncean Explorers (1949) put the issue into five judicial opinions about trapped cavers who killed one of their number to survive, showing that different philosophies of law lead to different results on the same facts. In the Hart-Fuller debate, published in the Harvard Law Review in 1958, Fuller defended his view against H. L. A. Hart's positivism, using among other examples the post-war prosecution of a woman who had denounced her husband under Nazi-era law. A West German court convicted her, reasoning that the statute was so contrary to the sound conscience of decent people that it was not binding. Hart thought it was better to say that the law was valid but too evil to obey and to punish her under a new retroactive statute, to avoid blurring the issues. Fuller thought the court's approach, or something like it, was better.

Gustav Radbruch, a German legal philosopher who had been a positivist before the war, reached a view often called the Radbruch formula after 1945. Positive law, secured by enactment and power, has priority even when unjust and contrary to the public interest, unless the conflict between statute and justice reaches an intolerable degree, in which case the statute must yield as flawed law. Extreme injustice is not law. German courts later referred to this idea in cases about East German border guards after reunification, an example of the continuing influence of the formula, though scholars debate how it was applied.

John Finnis, in Natural Law and Natural Rights (1980), offered a contemporary version rooted in Aquinas. He argued that there are basic goods that are self-evidently worth pursuing, including life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability or friendship, practical reasonableness and religion. Practical reasonableness yields requirements such as impartiality, respect for every basic value in every act, and promoting the common good. Law is a response to the need to coordinate action for the common good, and the central case of law is law that does this well. Unjust enactments are law in a derivative sense, and they lack the moral obligation that a just law has, though there may be reasons to comply to preserve the rule of law.

Critics say these theories confuse conceptual and moral claims, and that Fuller's principles are efficacy conditions common to any system of rules, including a ruthless one. Hart noted that poisoners need techniques too without poisoning being moral. Fuller's defenders respond that the principles of legality respect people as agents capable of following rules.

Worked example: a government secretly adopts rules, applies them retroactively, and changes them without notice. Fuller would say these officials are failing at law-making and moving away from law, a conclusion that a pure source-based theorist can accept as factual but would describe differently.

lessons.title: Bentham, Austin and the Command Theory
body: Legal positivism holds that the existence and content of law depend on social facts, not on moral merit. Its classical form was developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Austin. Bentham was a utilitarian who wanted law reformed according to the principle of utility, the greatest happiness of the greatest number, and he insisted on separating the description of law as it is from the criticism of law as it ought to be. He was impatient with common-law mystification and with judges who claimed to discover pre-existing law. He famously called the idea of natural rights, in the French Declaration, nonsense upon stilts. Bentham's scorn was not for justice but for the idea that moral claims could settle what the law is.

John Austin, in The Province of Jurisprudence Determined (1832), gave the standard command theory. Law, properly so called, is a command of a sovereign, backed by a threat of sanction, addressed to members of a political society. The sovereign is a person or body that is habitually obeyed by the bulk of the society and does not habitually obey anyone else. A command expresses a wish that others behave in a certain way and a power to harm them if they do not. Rules of positive morality, such as etiquette, and laws by analogy are not law in the strict sense. The theory has attractions: it is clear, descriptive, and explains law's coercive quality.

Austin separated law from morality: the existence of law is one thing, its merit or demerit another. This is the separation thesis in its classic form. He did not deny that unjust laws are bad. He denied that their badness changes their status. A judge may find a law abhorrent and still recognize it as law.

Hart's later critique, in The Concept of Law, argued that the command theory fails on several grounds. Many laws do not command at all but confer powers, such as the power to make a will or contract or to marry, and these are better seen as enabling rules than as orders backed by threats. Austin's sovereign makes the legislator seem to be above the law, but modern constitutional systems limit the legislature itself. The habit of obedience cannot explain the continuity of legal authority after a sovereign dies or is replaced, since a new ruler has no habit of obedience to build on, and yet laws continue to apply. Customary law, which does not originate in commands, becomes difficult to explain. And the theory cannot distinguish being obliged from having an obligation. Hart's example was a gunman who orders a bank clerk to hand over money: the clerk is obliged to comply, but the clerk has no obligation to do so in the sense that a legal duty involves.

Some defenders note that Bentham's own theory was more sophisticated than the textbook Austin, and that the command theory should be seen as a first step toward modern positivism rather than a position still defended. The core of Austin's insight, that law is a human artifact whose existence depends on social facts, remains central.

Worked example: a country's parliament passes a tax statute and the courts apply it. Under Austin, the statute is law because the sovereign commanded it and a sanction supports it. Hart would add that the statute is valid because it satisfies a rule of recognition that officials accept, which explains why a new parliament's statutes are also law even though its members were not the old sovereign.

lessons.title: Hart's The Concept of Law
body: H. L. A. Hart's The Concept of Law (1961) is the central text of modern positivism. Hart began from the failure of the command theory and offered a different picture: law is a system of rules, and what distinguishes a legal system from a mere set of orders is the union of primary and secondary rules.

Primary rules impose duties: do not steal, pay your taxes. A society with only primary rules, Hart said, would have three defects. The rules would be uncertain, because there would be no way to settle doubts about what they are. They would be static, because there would be no deliberate way to change them. And enforcement would be inefficient, because there would be no body authorized to settle disputes. The remedies are secondary rules. The rule of recognition identifies what counts as a valid rule of the system: it might say that whatever the legislature enacts, or whatever the constitution specifies, is law. Rules of change authorize the creation and repeal of rules. Rules of adjudication empower officials to determine whether a rule has been broken and to impose sanctions.

The rule of recognition is the ultimate criterion of validity, and it is a social rule, existing because officials actually practice it, taking an internal point of view. This is Hart's key distinction. From the external point of view an observer notes regularities of behavior and perhaps predicts penalties. From the internal point of view a participant accepts the rule as a standard of conduct and criticizes deviation from it. A legal system exists when ordinary people generally obey the primary rules and officials accept the secondary rules, especially the rule of recognition, as common standards for official behavior.

Hart also addressed open texture. Rules are expressed in general language, and general terms have a core of settled meaning and a penumbra where application is uncertain. A rule banning vehicles in a park clearly covers a truck, and it is unclear whether it covers a bicycle, a toy car or a war memorial tank. In the penumbra judges must exercise discretion, informed by purposes and consequences. For Hart this makes law incomplete, and in hard cases judges legislate interstitially, which he thought was a realistic and not a scandalous description.

Hart accepted a limited connection to natural law, which he called the minimum content of natural law. Given a few contingent facts about human beings (vulnerability, approximate equality, limited altruism, limited resources, and limited understanding and strength of will), any viable legal system will contain rules restricting violence, protecting property and enforcing promises. This explains why law and morality overlap without making the overlap conceptually necessary.

On the debate with Fuller, Hart held that the separation thesis does not mean laws are morally immune from criticism. It means we can recognize something as law and still condemn it. In his view this clarity is a moral advantage: if wicked laws are denied the name of law, people may conclude they need not think hard about resisting what is legal and wrong, or they may treat everything that is legal as morally binding.

Critics have pressed several points. Dworkin argued that Hart's picture cannot account for legal principles that bind judges. Others argue that practice-based accounts have trouble explaining disagreement among officials about the rule of recognition itself. Hart's Postscript, published after his death in 1994, answered Dworkin and allowed that a rule of recognition could incorporate moral criteria.

Worked example: a state's constitution says that statutes passed by the legislature and signed by the governor are law. Officials routinely treat such statutes as binding and criticize each other for departing from them. On Hart's account that practice is the rule of recognition, and a statute is valid by satisfying it, regardless of its fairness.

lessons.title: Kelsen, Raz and the Positivist Family
body: Positivism is a family of views, and contemporary debates concern which positivism is best. Hans Kelsen, an Austrian-born jurist who helped draft the Austrian constitution and later worked in the United States, developed the Pure Theory of Law (first edition 1934, second edition 1960). He aimed to purify legal science of politics, psychology, sociology and ethics, so that the study of law would describe norms without evaluating them. For Kelsen, a legal system is a hierarchy of norms in which each norm derives its validity from a higher norm, authorizing its creation. A court order is valid because a statute authorizes it, the statute because the constitution does, and the first constitution because of the Grundnorm, or basic norm, which is not itself posited but presupposed by legal science. The basic norm states that one ought to behave as the framers of the first constitution ordained. It is a transcendental presupposition that makes it possible to interpret the facts as law, and it is not a moral claim. Critics have asked whether this device explains anything, and whether a presupposed norm differs from Hart's social practice of officials. Kelsen also held that legal norms are acts of will and that interpretation of norms by courts is partly a matter of choice, not knowledge.

Joseph Raz, in The Authority of Law (1979), developed the sources thesis: the existence and content of law can be determined without moral argument, by reference to social sources such as legislation and precedent. His argument comes from the nature of authority. Law claims to have authority, and authority on his service conception works by giving reasons that replace the subject's own balance of reasons. If subjects had to weigh the merits to find out what an authority requires, the authority could not do its job of guiding action. Therefore the identification of law must be possible by factual means.

This produces the debate between exclusive and inclusive positivism. Exclusive positivists such as Raz hold that morality can never be a condition of legal validity. Inclusive, or soft, positivists such as Jules Coleman and Wil Waluchow hold that a legal system's rule of recognition may incorporate moral criteria, so that some constitutional clause such as a guarantee of equal protection makes morality a condition of validity in that system, yet the fact that it does so is a matter of social practice and not of conceptual necessity. Hart's Postscript endorsed the inclusive view. The dispute matters because it shows that positivism does not entail that morality is irrelevant in legal reasoning. It entails that morality is relevant only if and because the system makes it so.

Scott Shapiro's Legality (2011) offers a more recent theory, the planning theory, which treats law as a massive social planning activity aimed at solving problems that moral reasoning alone cannot settle, with the basic rules as plans that officials adopt. He argues that law's claim to settle moral questions explains its distinct institutional form.

A third line of positivist thought emphasizes normativity: how can a social fact give rise to a duty? Kelsen answers with the basic norm, Hart with the internal point of view, and Raz with the claim that law purports to create obligations without necessarily doing so.

Worked example: a constitution forbids "cruel and unusual" punishment. An exclusive positivist says a judge applying it must use social sources, such as the framers' intent and precedent, and when those run out she has discretion. An inclusive positivist says the clause makes moral evaluation part of what the law is. Both treat the existence of the clause as a social fact.

lessons.title: Dworkin and Law as Integrity
body: Ronald Dworkin presented the most influential challenge to positivism, first in an essay later reprinted in Taking Rights Seriously (1977) and then in Law's Empire (1986). His starting point was how judges actually reason in hard cases, where the explicit rules run out or conflict.

Dworkin distinguished rules from principles. Rules apply in an all-or-nothing fashion: if the facts are as the rule stipulates, then either the rule is valid and the answer it supplies must be accepted, or it is not. Principles, such as that no one should profit from his own wrong, have a dimension of weight and do not dictate results; they incline a decision in one direction and can be outweighed. In Riggs v. Palmer (New York, 1889), a grandson who murdered his grandfather to inherit under the will was held unable to take, although the statute of wills contained no exception. The court relied on the maxim that no one shall profit from his own wrong. Dworkin used this and Henningsen v. Bloomfield Motors (New Jersey, 1960), where the court limited a car maker's disclaimer by appeal to principles about fairness and public policy, to argue that law includes principles, and that principles are not valid by a pedigree test like Hart's rule of recognition, since they come from a sense of appropriateness developed over time. Hart's rule of recognition, he argued, cannot capture them.

From this Dworkin built the rights thesis: in hard cases judges should decide by identifying the rights that the parties have, not by making new policy, which is for legislatures. He also argued, controversially, that even in hard cases there is typically a right answer, though one that cannot be demonstrated beyond disagreement.

In Law's Empire he develops law as integrity. Judges should interpret the legal practice as a whole in the light that shows it as the best it can be, meeting two dimensions: fit with the past decisions and statutes, and justification in terms of moral and political principles. Adjudication is like adding a chapter to a chain novel, in which each author tries to make the whole text the best it can be while respecting what earlier authors wrote. His imagined judge, Hercules, is a superhuman judge with unlimited time who constructs the best theory of the law of his jurisdiction. Law's claim to be integrity expresses the ideal that a community should be governed by a single coherent vision of justice and fairness.

For Dworkin, law is an interpretive concept. Legal propositions are true in virtue of principles that provide the best justification of the legal practice, and so the question of what the law is cannot be separated from moral argument. He attacked what he called the semantic sting: the idea that legal disagreement must be a matter of different ideas about what the criteria for law are. For Dworkin the disagreement in real cases is often theoretical, about what the practice demands.

Critics say Dworkin's account overstates the determinacy of law, makes law too dependent on the judge's moral convictions, and gives judges too much power. Positivists reply that principles can be incorporated into law by a rule of recognition, a point Hart conceded in the Postscript. Raz argued that Dworkin's view confuses what a judge should do with what the law is. Dworkin's defenders respond that the debate shows that no neutral description of legal practice is possible.

Worked example: a statute grants an inheritance to "the child of the testator." The child has abused the testator for years. Dworkin says Hercules would ask which principles best fit and justify the practice of inheritance law, and might conclude the abuser should not take, in the same spirit as Riggs.

lessons.title: Legal Formalism and Legal Realism
body: Formalism, in the sense realists attacked, is the view that legal decisions follow logically from fixed rules and concepts, with little need for judges to consider policy. Its nineteenth-century American form is associated with Christopher Columbus Langdell, who developed the case method at Harvard and treated law as a science whose principles could be derived from the cases. The era of the Lochner decision (Lochner v. New York, 1905), in which the Supreme Court struck down a maximum-hours law for bakers by reference to liberty of contract, is often cited as the high point of formalist reasoning, though many scholars now argue that its judges were openly engaged in policy and that the label is somewhat caricatured.

Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. laid down the realist program in The Path of the Law (1897). He urged lawyers to look at law from the viewpoint of the bad man, who cares only about the material consequences of his conduct and wants to predict what courts will do. Law, in this prediction theory, is the prediction of the incidence of public force through the courts. He argued that judges' decisions reflect, whether they know it or not, the felt necessities of the time and their views of public policy, and that legal reasoning obscures this. His dissent in Lochner said that the Fourteenth Amendment did not enact a particular economic theory, and that a constitution is not meant to embody one.

American Legal Realism flourished in the 1920s and 1930s. Karl Llewellyn, author of The Bramble Bush (1930) and the article Some Realism About Realism (1931), argued that legal rules often underdetermine outcomes and that courts follow patterns of behavior best seen by studying what judges actually do. Jerome Frank, in Law and the Modern Mind (1930), emphasized that trials are uncertain not only because rules are uncertain but because facts are: witnesses err, juries are unpredictable, and judges are people with hunches. He is often called a fact-skeptic, in contrast to rule-skeptics who focused on indeterminate rules. The common claim that realists said judges decide by what they had for breakfast is a caricature; the realists generally said that judges are influenced by their social views and by how they see the facts. Realists also urged integrating social science into law and judging legal rules by their effects, a legacy visible in the policy analysis used in modern courts and in law and economics.

Hart's critique of rule-skepticism in The Concept of Law was that realists mistook predictability for the concept of law and ignored the internal point of view: officials treat the rules as reasons for decision, and the fact that some cases are indeterminate does not mean all are. Modern empirical studies of judicial behavior, including the attitudinal model in political science, find that ideology predicts votes in politically charged Supreme Court cases, while studies of ordinary trial and appellate cases find that law and doctrine constrain outcomes more often. Debate continues about how much law constrains judges.

Realism's influence persisted in legal process theory, in the policy-oriented jurisprudence of the New Haven school, and in the critical movements that followed, which radicalized the claim of indeterminacy.

Worked example: two courts apply the same precedent about a landlord's duty to repair and reach opposite results. A formalist says one court misapplied the logic. A realist asks what facts the judges saw, which policies moved them, and whether the cases differ in ways the rule cannot capture.

lessons.title: Theories of Interpretation
body: How should judges read a text? Theories of interpretation answer a question that every legal system faces, and each can be defended in terms of democratic legitimacy, stability, and fidelity to law.

Textualism holds that the statutory text, read in its ordinary meaning in context, is the law. Its defenders argue that legislatures enact texts, not intentions or purposes, that the legislative process of compromise would be undermined by judges who rely on unenacted purposes, and that focusing on text constrains judges and gives fair notice. Textualists use canons of construction and give limited weight to legislative history. In Bostock v. Clayton County (2020), the Supreme Court majority held that firing an employee for being gay or transgender is discrimination because of sex under Title VII, reasoning from the statute's ordinary meaning that the employer must take sex into account. The opinion was by Justice Gorsuch, a textualist, and the dissenters, who also emphasized text and the ordinary meaning of the words at the time of enactment, concluded otherwise, showing that a shared method does not guarantee agreement.

Originalism holds that the Constitution's meaning is fixed when it is adopted. Early versions stressed the framers' intentions, but the dominant form today, original public meaning, asks how a reasonable reader at the time would have understood the words. Its defenders argue that fixed meaning is needed for law to constrain, that legitimate change comes through amendment, and that otherwise unelected judges update the Constitution to match their views. In District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), the Court majority and the dissent both relied heavily on eighteenth-century history in disagreeing about whether the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep arms for self-defense, which shows that originalist method does not remove disagreement and that historians and lawyers read evidence differently.

Purposivism holds that statutes should be read in light of their purposes, as the legislature would reasonably have understood them. Henry Hart and Albert Sacks's legal process materials proposed that judges should imagine the reasonable legislature pursuing reasonable purposes reasonably. Purposivists use committee reports and statutory context and accept that language is imperfect. Critics say that purposes are found at levels of abstraction that allow judges to choose.

Living constitutionalism holds that constitutional meaning evolves as society changes, through precedent, practice and changing moral understanding. David Strauss's common-law constitutionalism argues that the Constitution's meaning is developed in the way the common law is, constrained by precedent and by humility. The Court's opinions on cruel and unusual punishment have said that the clause draws its meaning from the evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society, a formula used, for example, in the juvenile death penalty decision Roper v. Simmons (2005). Critics say this gives judges too much power and weakens constraint. Defenders say that rigid originalism produces results nobody accepts and that precedent and tradition provide discipline.

Pragmatism, associated with Richard Posner, evaluates interpretations by their consequences, while Stephen Breyer's active liberty approach emphasizes democratic participation. Dworkin's moral reading says abstract constitutional clauses should be read as asking moral questions.

Worked example: a town ordinance bans "vehicles" in a park and a veterans' group wishes to display a restored military truck as a monument. A textualist notes that a truck is plainly a vehicle but asks whether context suggests an exception. A purposivist asks what mischief the ordinance targeted, namely noise and danger, and would likely allow a static display. Each method has an account of why it is the right way to read.

lessons.title: Critical Legal Studies
body: Critical Legal Studies (CLS) emerged in the United States in the late 1970s, after a conference at the University of Wisconsin in 1977, among law teachers who combined the realists' skepticism with ideas from Marxism, the Frankfurt School, structuralism and later postmodernism. Leading figures include Roberto Unger, Duncan Kennedy, Mark Kelman, Morton Horwitz and Karl Klare. It was less a unified theory than a stance.

The core claims can be set out in order. The first is the indeterminacy thesis: legal doctrine is contradictory enough, and general principles open enough, that it does not by itself determine the outcome of most cases. Strong versions say that for any case the available materials permit arguments both ways; moderate versions say indeterminacy is widespread and concentrated in contested areas. Scholars used a method sometimes called trashing, taking apart the reasoning of doctrines to show that they rest on opposed principles. Kennedy's Form and Substance in Private Law Adjudication (1976) argued that private law is organized around a conflict between individualism and altruism, and that no neutral reasoning can resolve it.

The second claim is that law is politics and ideology. If doctrine does not determine results, judges choose, and the choices tend to reflect and reinforce the existing social hierarchy while presenting it as natural and necessary. Law helps legitimate arrangements by making them look neutral and by shaping how people see what is possible. The liberal distinction between public and private spheres, for example, was said to hide the fact that decisions to leave matters to private ordering are themselves political decisions made by the state.

The third claim is a critique of liberal legalism, including rights discourse. Some critics argued that rights are indeterminate and protect existing distributions, while others thought rights talk could be useful for subordinated groups. Some CLS scholars, notably Unger, argued for constructive projects such as imagining institutional alternatives and empowering people to revise the arrangements of their society, which he called a program of deviationist doctrine and superliberalism.

CLS was criticized from several sides. Liberal theorists such as Dworkin argued that law has more structure than CLS allows, and that an interpretive practice constrains even when it does not determine. Positivists and empirical scholars noted that most legal questions in ordinary life have clear answers, which indeterminacy theorists tend to underplay, and that lawyers and clients depend on predictability. Others said that CLS lacked a positive program or that its critique of rights was dangerous to the groups that most need them. These last concerns were pressed by scholars of color and feminists who were sympathetic to critique but wanted to retain the language of rights, a dispute that fed into the emergence of critical race theory and feminist jurisprudence.

CLS declined as an organized movement in the 1990s, but its themes persist in legal scholarship: the claim that law is not autonomous from politics, attention to the way framing choices distribute power, and critical studies of the family, labor and property.

Worked example: a court must decide whether a landlord's duty to maintain a rental unit overrides the tenant's contract to accept the unit as is. CLS says that either result can be defended through principles, freedom of contract on one side and protection of the vulnerable on the other, and that the choice expresses a political view about the proper balance, whatever the opinion's language of neutrality. A liberal theorist responds that precedent and principle still narrow the choices.

lessons.title: Critical Race Theory
body: Critical Race Theory (CRT) is a body of scholarship that began in American law schools in the late 1970s and 1980s, associated with Derrick Bell, Alan Freeman, Kimberlé Crenshaw, Richard Delgado, Mari Matsuda, Patricia Williams, Charles Lawrence and others. Several began in Critical Legal Studies and broke away because they thought CLS neglected race and undervalued the practical importance of civil rights. CRT is a legal-academic movement, and its ideas have been the subject of public controversy outside the academy, where the term is often used in broader and different senses.

Its main themes can be described in the movement's own terms. First, racism is not only individual prejudice but is often embedded in institutions, laws and practices, and may persist without intent. Second, race is a social construction, not a biological category, yet it has real effects. Third, Bell's interest-convergence thesis, from the article Brown v. Board of Education and the Interest-Convergence Dilemma (1980), holds that advances for Black Americans tend to occur when they also serve the interests of white elites. Bell argued that the Brown decision's timing was connected to Cold War foreign policy concerns and the interest in economic development in the South. Fourth, critics of colorblindness argue that formal neutrality can lock in existing disparities, because race-neutral rules operating on unequal conditions reproduce inequality. Fifth, many CRT writers use storytelling and counter-narrative, including personal and fictional narratives, to bring experiences outside the dominant account into legal discourse. Delgado's Storytelling for Oppositionists and Others (1989) argued that stories can challenge the majoritarian narrative.

Crenshaw's Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex (1989) introduced intersectionality, the idea that the experience of discrimination against Black women is not captured by considering race and sex separately. Her example was a lawsuit in which a court rejected a claim that a firm discriminated against Black women, because the firm hired white women for secretarial jobs and Black men for industrial jobs, and so no discrimination on either axis was shown. Intersectionality has spread well beyond law.

CRT writers differ about law. Some, like Bell in later work, were pessimistic about the permanence of racism and the limits of legal reform, while others, like Matsuda, emphasized the role of law in redress and the role of hate speech regulation. Their view of rights is generally more favorable than that of Critical Legal Studies, because rights have been useful to people of color historically.

Critics raise a number of objections. Randall Kennedy, a sympathetic critic, argued in 1989 that some CRT claims about the quality of minority scholarship and about the alleged bias of standard academic evaluation lack evidence. Daniel Farber and Suzanna Sherry criticized storytelling as a form of argument that is hard to evaluate. Others, including some liberal and conservative commentators, argue that CRT's focus on group identity and structural explanations undermines individual responsibility and universal principles like colorblindness and merit. They also dispute claims about interest convergence. Supporters respond that universal principles in practice have not delivered equality, and that CRT is a tool for identifying structural patterns. Since 2021 a number of US states have adopted laws restricting how certain concepts about race may be taught in public schools, with the scope of what is covered varying by state and with ongoing litigation.

Worked example: a hiring test, neutral on its face, screens out disproportionate numbers of Black applicants and is not strongly job-related. Under Griggs v. Duke Power Co. (1971), the disparate-impact doctrine allows such practices to be challenged without proof of intent, an application consistent with the structural view that neutral rules can have discriminatory effects.

lessons.title: Feminist Jurisprudence
body: Feminist jurisprudence asks how law treats women and gender, and whether law's apparently neutral concepts reflect men's experience. It is not one theory but a family of approaches that disagree sharply with one another, and it is best understood by its main strands.

Liberal feminism, the earliest strand in modern law, argues for formal and substantive equality of opportunity: women should be treated as individuals, without sex stereotypes. Its legal triumphs include Reed v. Reed (1971), in which the Supreme Court for the first time struck down a sex-based classification under the Equal Protection Clause, a preference for male administrators of estates, and later cases in which the Court applied intermediate scrutiny. United States v. Virginia (1996) held that the exclusion of women from the Virginia Military Institute needed an exceedingly persuasive justification and was not met. Liberal feminists defend the ideals of neutrality and individual rights and argue that law has failed to live up to them.

Difference or cultural feminism emphasizes that women's experiences and values may differ from men's and should be recognized, not erased. Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice (1982), a work in psychology, argued that many women reason in an ethic of care in contrast to an ethic of justice, and influenced legal scholars. Robin West's Jurisprudence and Gender (1988) argued that mainstream jurisprudence takes a masculine view of the person as separate, and neglects connection, such as the experience of pregnancy and nurturing. Critics worry that this approach risks reinforcing stereotypes and that the empirical claims about difference are contested.

Dominance feminism, developed by Catharine MacKinnon in Feminism Unmodified (1987) and Toward a Feminist Theory of the State (1989), argues that the central issue is not sameness or difference but power: gender is a hierarchy in which men dominate women, and law that treats women as the same as or different from men, measured by a male standard, will reproduce that hierarchy. MacKinnon's work led to the legal concept of sexual harassment as sex discrimination, a view adopted by the Supreme Court in Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson (1986), which held that a hostile work environment can violate Title VII. MacKinnon and Andrea Dworkin also drafted ordinances treating pornography as a civil-rights violation; the Indianapolis version was held unconstitutional under the First Amendment in American Booksellers Association v. Hudnut (7th Cir. 1985). The dispute shows a tension between feminist legal aims and free speech principles, and some feminists opposed the ordinances.

Anti-essentialist and intersectional critiques, such as Angela Harris's Race and Essentialism in Feminist Legal Theory (1990), argue that generalizations about women often reflect the experiences of white, middle-class women, and that theories must account for how race, class and sexuality shape women's lives. Postmodern feminists question stable categories of sex and gender altogether. Susan Moller Okin's Justice, Gender and the Family (1989) argued that theories of justice such as Rawls's overlook the family as a site of inequality.

Critics from outside feminism argue that the dominance approach treats too many matters as power relations and neglects women's agency. Some critics also say that categorical claims about male power fit poorly with differences among men.

Worked example: an employer's policy denies benefits for pregnancy-related disability while covering other disabilities. A liberal approach asks whether pregnancy is like other conditions and demands equal treatment, a difference approach asks whether law must accommodate women's distinct biology, and a dominance approach asks whether the policy sustains women's subordination at work. These differences explain disputes within feminist legal theory.

lessons.title: Law and Economics
body: Law and economics applies economic methods, especially the analysis of incentives and efficiency, to legal rules. Its modern growth began with Ronald Coase's The Problem of Social Cost (1960), Guido Calabresi's work on accidents, and Richard Posner's Economic Analysis of Law (1973). It can be positive, explaining the content and effects of legal rules, or normative, recommending rules that promote efficiency.

The Coase theorem states that if transaction costs are zero and property rights are well defined, bargaining will lead to an efficient allocation of resources regardless of how the law initially assigns rights. Coase's point was that transaction costs are never zero in practice, so the law's allocation of rights matters and courts should consider which assignment results in the lowest overall cost. His example of a rancher whose cattle trample a neighbor's crops illustrates that who is liable can be irrelevant to the use of land if bargaining is costless, and decisive when it is not.

Calabresi and Melamed's article of 1972, Property Rules, Liability Rules, and Inalienability, proposed a framework: an entitlement can be protected by a property rule, which allows transfer only through voluntary exchange, by a liability rule, which allows taking at a court-determined price, or by inalienability. In Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co. (New York, 1970), neighbors sued a cement plant for nuisance, and the court held that the plant could continue if it paid permanent damages, a liability-rule solution instead of an injunction, and the case is a staple of the framework.

Efficiency has several meanings. A change is Pareto efficient if it makes someone better off without making anyone worse off. Because few changes meet this test, most analysis uses Kaldor-Hicks efficiency: a change is efficient if the winners could compensate the losers and still be better off, whether or not compensation is paid. Posner defended wealth maximization as a normative standard for the common law, arguing that judges tend to produce efficient rules.

A classic application is negligence. In United States v. Carroll Towing Co. (Second Circuit, 1947), Judge Learned Hand suggested that a defendant is negligent if the burden of precautions is less than the probability of harm multiplied by the magnitude of the loss: B less than P times L. Courts do not usually compute this formula numerically, but it captures the cost-benefit logic of negligence.

Critics make several points. The distributional objection says efficiency ignores who gets what, and willingness to pay reflects wealth. Dworkin's essay Is Wealth a Value? (1980) argued that wealth maximization is not an adequate moral standard because wealth is not itself valuable. Others say that economic analysis assumes rational preferences, and behavioral law and economics, drawing on psychology and the work of Kahneman and Tversky, shows systematic departures such as loss aversion and overconfidence, so law may need to account for them, as in Jolls, Sunstein and Thaler's 1998 article. Another objection is that the approach cannot explain rights that are non-market, such as basic liberties. Defenders respond that efficiency is one value among others and that economic analysis reveals the costs of legal choices whatever one's moral view.

Worked example: a factory emits smoke that harms a dozen nearby homeowners. Coasean analysis asks whether bargaining is feasible. With twelve owners, holdout and organizational costs may block a deal, so a court might choose between an injunction and damages by asking which rule produces the more efficient outcome, as in Boomer. A critic asks whose interests were left out of the calculation.

lessons.title: The Rule of Law
body: The rule of law is one of the most praised and least agreed-upon ideas in politics. At its simplest it means that government is itself bound by law and that no one is above it. The question for jurisprudence is what else is included, and the answer separates formal, or thin, conceptions from substantive, or thick, ones.

A.V. Dicey, in Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885), gave a classic British formulation with three elements: the supremacy of regular law as against arbitrary power; equality before the law, with officials subject to the same ordinary courts as everyone else; and the idea that constitutional rights result from ordinary judicial decisions and not from a charter. His account has been criticized for ignoring the administrative state, but its emphasis on legal limits on officials remains. The eighteenth-century case Entick v. Carrington (1765) is often cited as an example: the court held that the king's messengers could not enter and search a home and seize papers without legal authority, rejecting the claim of state necessity.

Fuller's eight principles of legality, discussed earlier, supply a procedural account: laws should be general, public, prospective, clear, consistent, possible to follow, stable and applied as announced. Joseph Raz in The Rule of Law and Its Virtue (1977) gave a formal account with principles such as prospective, open and clear laws, relatively stable laws, guidance of particular laws by open, general rules, independence of the judiciary, natural justice, review power by courts, accessible courts, and limits on the discretion of crime-preventing agencies. For Raz, the rule of law is a virtue of legal systems, like the sharpness of a knife, which can be used for good or ill. A legal system that violates basic human rights might conform to the rule of law, and so the rule of law is not the whole of political morality.

Substantive conceptions add moral content. Dworkin's rights conception holds that the rule of law is the ideal of rule by an accurate public conception of individual rights, so that citizens can claim rights in courts. Lord Bingham in The Rule of Law (2010) proposed eight principles, including that law must be accessible, intelligible, clear and predictable; that questions of legal right should normally be decided by law and not discretion; that laws apply equally; that law must protect fundamental human rights; that means must be provided for resolving disputes without prohibitive cost; that public officials must act reasonably and within their powers; that the state must comply with its international obligations; and that adjudicative procedures must be fair. Critics of thick views say they merge the rule of law with justice generally, losing a distinct ideal that appeals across political disagreements.

Friedrich Hayek, in The Road to Serfdom (1944) and The Constitution of Liberty (1960), argued from a classical-liberal perspective that general, predictable rules protect individual freedom from arbitrary state power, and that economic planning threatens it.

A related distinction is between rule of law and rule by law. In rule by law, law is merely an instrument used by rulers, which authoritarian regimes can use to govern efficiently without being bound by it. In rule of law, rulers are constrained by it. The World Justice Project and other organizations publish indices that measure the rule of law across countries on factors such as constraints on government power and absence of corruption, which are used in policy debates, though measurement is itself contested.

Worked example: a government secretly issues a regulation, applies it to conduct that occurred before its publication, and punishes officials who refuse to enforce it. A thin account identifies failures of publicity, prospectivity and consistent application. A thick account adds that if the regulation also stripped a minority of basic rights, it would fail the rule of law even if it had been published and applied evenly.

lessons.title: Theories of Punishment
body: Why may the state inflict suffering on an offender? Punishment needs justification because it involves the deliberate imposition of harm. The main theories answer from different starting points, and most modern systems blend them.

Retributivism holds that wrongdoers deserve punishment because they have done wrong, and that the punishment should be proportionate to the offense and the offender's culpability. The justification looks backward, to the offense. Kant argued that punishment must never be used merely as a means to some other good for the offender or society, and that it is imposed because the offender has committed a crime; he used the example of a society on an island that must execute its last murderer before dissolving. Hegel saw punishment as the negation of the negation of right, treating the criminal as a rational being who is honored by being held responsible. Modern retributivists such as Michael Moore defend desert as a moral basis, while others emphasize fair play: the offender has taken an unfair advantage over law-abiding citizens, and punishment restores the balance. Retributivism supplies proportionality and limits on punishing the innocent, but critics ask why suffering is intrinsically good and how to measure desert.

Consequentialist theories justify punishment by its good effects. Bentham and utilitarians stress deterrence: punishment deters the offender (specific deterrence) and others (general deterrence), by raising the expected cost of crime. Incapacitation protects the public by preventing offenders from committing crimes while confined. Rehabilitation aims to change the offender through treatment, education or training. Consequentialist theories are forward-looking, and critics argue that they could justify punishing the innocent or imposing disproportionate sentences if doing so would deter, or treat people as mere means. Empirical research shows that the certainty of detection tends to deter more than the severity of punishment, though the evidence is mixed and contested in detail.

Hart's Prolegomenon to the Principles of Punishment (1959) proposed a mixed view that distinguishes the general justifying aim of punishment, which for Hart is the utilitarian one of reducing crime, from the principles of distribution, which limit who may be punished and how much, drawing on retributive principles such as the requirement of guilt and proportionality. Rawls in Two Concepts of Rules (1955) made a related distinction between justifying a practice and justifying a particular act within it.

Expressive theories, such as Joel Feinberg's 1965 essay The Expressive Function of Punishment, hold that punishment communicates society's condemnation of the conduct, and that this expressive meaning is part of what distinguishes punishment from a mere penalty. Communicative theories, such as R. A. Duff's, say that punishment is an attempt to engage the offender in moral dialogue and elicit repentance. Restorative justice focuses on repairing harm to victims and communities and on offender accountability, through mediation and conferencing. Abolitionist critics argue that prisons cause more harm than they prevent and that alternatives should replace them.

Capital punishment is a controversial practice, and the arguments should be kept apart from the law. As a matter of current US law, the death penalty is constitutional, but the Supreme Court has limited its use: Furman v. Georgia (1972) struck down the then-existing statutes for arbitrary application, Gregg v. Georgia (1976) upheld new guided-discretion statutes, Atkins v. Virginia (2002) barred execution of people with intellectual disability, Roper v. Simmons (2005) barred execution of those who were under eighteen at the time of the crime, and Kennedy v. Louisiana (2008) barred it for the rape of a child that did not result in death. Many states and most of the world's countries have abolished it, and a number of states retain it by statute but have not carried out executions for years. Supporters rely mainly on retributive reasons and sometimes deterrence, and opponents rely on risk of error, uneven application, and the view that the state should not take life.

Worked example: a defendant who steals a loaf of bread for a starving child is given a long sentence to deter others. A retributivist objects that it is disproportionate, while a pure deterrence theorist must rely on empirical claims about effects. Hart's mixed view would cap the sentence by proportionality.

lessons.title: Justice as Fairness: Rawls
body: John Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971) revived political philosophy and set the terms for later debate. His problem was to identify principles of justice for the basic structure of society, the main institutions that distribute rights, duties and advantages. His method was social contract: principles of justice are those that free and equal persons would agree to in a fair initial situation.

That situation is the original position, a hypothetical device. Parties choose principles behind a veil of ignorance: they do not know their place in society, class, race, sex, natural abilities, conception of the good, or the generation they belong to, but they know general facts about psychology and economics. The veil ensures that no one can tailor principles to their advantage. Rawls argued that rational parties would choose two principles, with the first having priority over the second. The first principle says each person has an equal claim to a fully adequate scheme of equal basic liberties compatible with the same liberties for all. The second says social and economic inequalities must satisfy two conditions: they must be attached to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity, and they must be to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society, which is the difference principle.

Rawls argued that parties in the original position would use a conservative decision rule, close to maximin, which ranks alternatives by their worst outcomes, because the stakes are high and the probabilities unknown. This is a central point of contention. John Harsanyi argued that rational parties would instead maximize expected average utility, which would support a utilitarian principle. Rawls replied that utilitarianism fails to respect the separateness of persons, since it allows the sacrifice of some for the larger benefit of others.

The method of reflective equilibrium adjusts principles and considered judgments about particular cases until they cohere. In his later work, Political Liberalism (1993), Rawls recast justice as fairness as a political conception, not a comprehensive moral doctrine, which could be supported by an overlapping consensus of reasonable but conflicting religious and philosophical views in a pluralist society. He also developed the idea of public reason, that in debates about constitutional essentials citizens should offer reasons that others can accept.

Rawls has been criticized from many directions. Robert Nozick, in the next lesson, argued from libertarian premises. Communitarians such as Michael Sandel argued that the self in the original position is an unencumbered self, detached from the attachments that constitute people's identities. Feminist critics, including Susan Moller Okin, argued that Rawls does not apply the principles to the family. Others argue that the theory idealizes by focusing on perfectly just institutions and that it does not address global justice adequately, although Rawls's The Law of Peoples (1999) addressed international justice in a way many found less demanding than the domestic theory. Critics from the left have said that the difference principle does not go far enough in preventing concentrations of wealth, and Rawls himself discussed property-owning democracy as a more suitable regime than welfare-state capitalism.

The relevance to law lies in constitutional design, antidiscrimination law, taxation, and the idea that institutions must be justifiable to all citizens. Rawls is not a legal theorist, but his theory has been cited and debated by legal scholars and, less often, referred to in judicial opinions.

Worked example: a legislature considers a tax policy that boosts the economy and raises average incomes, while lowering the income of the poorest decile. A utilitarian might support it if total welfare rises. Rawls's difference principle would reject it unless the inequality improved the position of the least advantaged compared with the alternatives.

lessons.title: Nozick, Sen and Other Accounts of Justice
body: Rawls is one contributor to a wide debate. This lesson sets out other major accounts, each in its own terms, so that they can be compared.

Robert Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) is the leading libertarian answer. Starting from the premise that individuals have rights that no one may violate, Nozick argued that only a minimal state, limited to protection against force, theft and fraud and enforcement of contracts, is justified; a more extensive state violates rights. His theory of distributive justice is the entitlement theory, which is historical and unpatterned. A distribution is just if it arises from a just initial acquisition of holdings, just transfers, and rectification of past injustices in acquisition or transfer. He contrasted this with end-state and patterned principles, which hold that a distribution is just if it matches some pattern such as equality, because maintaining a pattern requires continuous interference. His Wilt Chamberlain example imagines a population in a distribution that satisfies any pattern one favors, and that many people each pay a small sum to watch a famous basketball player play; the resulting distribution, he said, is unequal but is the result of voluntary transfers, so any pattern would be disrupted by free exchange. He argued that taxation of earnings from labor is on a par with forced labor, a controversial claim.

Critics ask whether original acquisition of unowned things can be justified, given Locke's proviso that enough and as good be left for others, and how rectification should work given the history of conquest and slavery. G. A. Cohen argued that self-ownership, as Nozick conceives it, does not support the conclusion that property rights in external resources are absolute. Others note that the theory has little to say about the claims of those who start with very few resources, and that it depends on a strong premise about rights.

Amartya Sen's The Idea of Justice (2009) criticizes what he calls transcendental institutionalism, the approach of Rawls and others that seeks perfectly just institutions, and favors a comparative approach that asks how to reduce clear injustices and rank alternatives. He illustrated this with the story of three children who dispute who should get a flute: one can play it, one has no other toys, and one made it. Each of them has a reasoned claim, based on different principles, utilitarian, egalitarian and entitlement, and no single principle is obviously correct, yet one can often reach agreement that a certain change would reduce injustice. Sen is a central figure in the capability approach, developed with Martha Nussbaum, which holds that justice should be measured by what people are actually able to do and to be, their capabilities, rather than by resources or utility. Nussbaum proposed a list of central capabilities, including life, bodily health, bodily integrity, practical reason and affiliation, as the basis for constitutional guarantees. Critics ask whether the approach is specific enough to guide institutions, and who decides which capabilities count.

Aristotle's account, in Book V of the Nicomachean Ethics, distinguishes distributive justice, concerned with the fair division of honors and goods in proportion to merit or desert, and corrective justice, which restores equality after a wrong, as in tort and contract. Corrective justice theories of private law, associated with Ernest Weinrib and Jules Coleman, build on this.

Utilitarianism, from Bentham and John Stuart Mill, holds that the right act or rule maximizes overall welfare. Its defenders emphasize impartiality and concern with consequences, while critics emphasize that it may sacrifice individuals and ignore rights. Michael Walzer's Spheres of Justice (1983) argued that different goods, such as office, money and education, should be distributed by different principles, appropriate to their social meaning, and that justice means preventing domination by one sphere over others.

Worked example: a city has a parcel of land and three claimants: a developer who owns adjoining land, a group of homeless residents who need housing, and a community that made the park there. Nozick asks about the history of title. Rawls asks what arrangement would benefit the least advantaged. Sen asks how to reduce the most remediable injustice, and the capability approach asks what people can do and be.

lessons.title: Law and Morality: Enforcing Morals, Obedience and Civil Disobedience
body: Even if law and morality are conceptually separate, the question remains how they should relate in practice. Should law enforce morality as such? Is there a duty to obey the law? When may a person disobey?

The modern debate began with the Wolfenden Report (1957) in Britain, which recommended that homosexual acts between consenting adults in private and prostitution not be criminal offenses, on the ground that the function of criminal law is to preserve public order and protect citizens from what is offensive or injurious, not to enforce a particular pattern of moral behavior. Patrick Devlin, a judge, responded in his 1959 lecture The Enforcement of Morals that a society is held together by a shared morality, and that law may enforce it, because society may protect itself against disintegration, as it does against treason. He argued that the limits are tolerance, privacy and the standard of the reasonable person's reaction of intolerance, indignation and disgust. Hart replied in Law, Liberty and Morality (1963), invoking John Stuart Mill's harm principle from On Liberty (1859): the only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over any member of a civilized community against his will is to prevent harm to others. Hart argued that Devlin offered no evidence that deviation from conventional morality threatens a society's existence, and that enforcing morality can itself cause suffering. Hart accepted some paternalism, such as laws limiting consent to harm.

Joel Feinberg's four-volume The Moral Limits of the Criminal Law (1984-88) refined the debate by defending the harm principle, supplemented by an offense principle for serious public nuisances, and rejecting legal moralism and most paternalism. Legal moralists such as Michael Moore defend the claim that immorality, even without harm to others, can be a reason for criminalization if it is wrongful. The question is alive in debates about drug laws, assisted dying and obscenity, where participants dispute what counts as harm and who is harmed. In US constitutional law, Bowers v. Hardwick (1986) upheld a Georgia sodomy statute partly on the ground that majority morality can be a legitimate basis for law; Lawrence v. Texas (2003) overruled Bowers and struck down a similar statute, holding that the state's interest in the morality of the practice was not sufficient. Debates among commentators about the roles of harm and morality continued in those opinions.

On the duty to obey, Plato's Crito presents Socrates arguing that he owes obedience to the laws of Athens because they raised and protected him, an early consent and gratitude argument. Modern theorists give various grounds: fairness, because those who benefit from a cooperative scheme should do their share; consent, hard to show for most citizens; natural duty to support just institutions (Rawls); and associative obligations (Dworkin). Raz argued that there is no general obligation to obey even a legitimate government, though there may be reasons to comply in many cases. Philosophical anarchists such as Robert Paul Wolff argue that the duty is incompatible with autonomy.

Civil disobedience is public, nonviolent, conscientious law-breaking to bring about change, in Rawls's formulation, directed at a society that is nearly just. Henry David Thoreau's essay (1849) defended refusing to pay taxes in protest against slavery and war. Martin Luther King Jr.'s Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963) argued that one has a moral responsibility to disobey unjust laws, citing Augustine's view that an unjust law is no law at all and Aquinas, while insisting that the disobedient must act openly and accept the penalty. In Walker v. City of Birmingham (1967), the Supreme Court, five to four, upheld contempt convictions of King and others for marching in violation of an injunction, without reaching the claim that the injunction was invalid, since they had not first sought to challenge it in court.

Worked example: a city bans overnight camping in parks, and activists camp in defiance to draw attention to homelessness, notify police in advance, and accept arrest. Under Rawls's criteria this may qualify as civil disobedience, whereas a violent or secret act would not, whatever one thinks about the cause.

lessons.title: The Nature of Rights
body: Talk of rights is everywhere in law, but the word is used loosely. Wesley Hohfeld, in Some Fundamental Legal Conceptions as Applied in Judicial Reasoning (1913) and a second article in 1917, argued that what people call a right can mean four different things, and that clarity requires separating them. His scheme has eight terms in two groups of correlatives and opposites.

A claim-right, or right in the strict sense, correlates with a duty in another: if you have a right that I not trespass on your land, I have a duty not to. Its opposite is a no-right. A privilege, now often called a liberty, is the absence of a duty, correlating with a no-right in others: I have a privilege to walk on my own land, meaning I have no duty not to, and you cannot complain. A power is the ability to change legal relations, such as the power to sell property, make a will or form a contract, correlating with liability in the person whose relations are changed, and its opposite is disability. An immunity is freedom from having one's legal relations changed by another, correlating with disability: a person immune from suit cannot have the power to be sued exercised on her. By separating these, Hohfeld showed that a statement such as "the press has a right to publish" can mean a liberty, a claim against interference, an immunity from regulation, or a power, which have different consequences in a case.

Two theories compete about what rights are for. The will or choice theory, associated with Hart and, in different forms, with Kant and Savigny, holds that to have a right is to have control over another's duty: the right-holder can waive, enforce or release it. The interest theory, defended by Bentham, Ihering and, in modern form, Joseph Raz and Neil MacCormick, holds that a right exists when an aspect of the right-holder's well-being is a sufficient reason for holding another to a duty. The theories differ on cases: children and incompetent persons seem to have rights though they cannot waive them, which favors the interest theory, while the will theory has trouble with inalienable rights such as the prohibition on slavery, and the interest theory has trouble saying why a third-party beneficiary of a contract's promise lacks a right.

Dworkin's essay Rights as Trumps (1984) proposed that rights are political trumps held by individuals, which defeat the usual justification of collective goals. Rights, on his view, mark limits on what governments may do in the name of the general welfare.

The source of rights is another issue. Natural rights theorists such as Locke argued that individuals have rights prior to government, and that government exists to protect them. Legal positivists tend to say that legal rights are those the law recognizes, and that moral rights are a separate matter. Human rights are rights held by all persons as such, and in the international system they are stated in documents such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), a General Assembly declaration and not a treaty, and in the International Covenants on Civil and Political Rights and on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (both 1966), which are binding treaties for the states that have ratified them.

Rights have had critics. Bentham called natural rights nonsense and imprescriptible natural rights nonsense upon stilts, because he held that real rights are created by law. Burke attacked the abstract rights of man in favor of the inherited rights of Englishmen. Marx, in On the Jewish Question (1843), argued that the rights of man are rights of egoistic individuals separate from community. Alasdair MacIntyre in After Virtue (1981) said that belief in natural rights is like belief in witches and unicorns. Defenders reply that rights are ordinary and useful moral tools, and that rights discourse has protected the vulnerable. Communitarian and feminist writers ask for rights to be balanced by relationships and responsibilities.

Worked example: a tenant has a lease. Her claim-right to quiet enjoyment correlates with the landlord's duty not to interfere. Her liberty to have guests means the landlord has no right to forbid them. She has a power to renew or assign the lease if permitted. And she has an immunity from eviction without notice, correlating with the landlord's disability to terminate without it.

lessons.title: How Philosophy Shows Up Inside Real Opinions
body: Judges rarely cite philosophers, but their opinions use jurisprudential arguments constantly. Reading a case with the vocabulary of this course makes visible moves that otherwise pass as plain reasoning. This lesson gives a field guide with real examples and also warns against over-labelling.

Positivism and the plain law. When a judge says that a statute must be applied as written even though the result is harsh, and that relief is for the legislature, she is endorsing a separation between what the law is and what it should be. A judge who invokes the plain meaning rule or who refuses to read in an exception is assuming that the text's meaning is determined by the social fact of enactment. In Bostock, both the majority and the dissent proceeded from the text of Title VII and disagreed about its ordinary meaning, which illustrates that agreement on theory does not produce agreement on outcome.

Principles and integrity. In Riggs v. Palmer (1889), the New York Court of Appeals decided that a murderer could not inherit under his victim's will, although the statute set no exception, on the ground that no one should profit from his own wrong. Dworkin read this as a principle operating beside the rules. A court that fills a gap by appeal to fairness or the purpose of the doctrine is doing something Dworkin describes as integrity, and a positivist describes as discretion or incorporated moral standards, depending on the version.

Natural law and the higher law. The Declaration of Independence invoked laws of nature. The Nuremberg tribunals rejected defences of superior orders and legality under the Nazi regime for crimes against humanity, and German courts after the war and after reunification faced the problem of retrospectively judging acts that were lawful when done, in which the Radbruch formula and positivist replies were both used by courts and scholars. Justice Harlan's dissent in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) said that the Constitution is color-blind and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens, a principle drawing on a conception of equal citizenship above the statute.

Realism and consequences. Holmes's Lochner dissent (1905) said that the case was decided on an economic theory the majority held, which a constitution does not enact. Brown v. Board of Education (1954) relied on social-science evidence about the effects of segregation on children, a realist approach, although the weight the Court placed on the evidence is debated. A judge who weighs the likely consequences of a rule is practicing something the realists encouraged.

Law and economics. In Carroll Towing (1947), Judge Hand's formula for negligence compares the burden of precautions to the expected loss, which is law and economics before the label. In Boomer v. Atlantic Cement (1970), the court weighed the cost of closing the plant against the harm to neighbors and chose damages.
